title: You haven't been there (Avot 2:4)
hookLine: Hillel: don't separate from the community; don't judge until you've stood in their place

lines: THE MOTHER IN THE CHECKOUT LINE.
cards: The woman in the checkout line snaps at her kid, and everyone around her silently decides what kind of mother she is. The coworker who's been late three times this month. The neighbor who never mows his lawn.
These verdicts arrive in an instant, and they feel very sure. What nobody sees is the hospital visit that morning, or the second job, or the thing nobody talks about at home.
Hillel, the gentle sage from the roof in the snow, has five short warnings in chapter two. The middle one is about exactly this.

teach.b: Here they are. Don't separate yourself from the community. Don't be sure of yourself until the day you die.

Don't judge your fellow until you've reached his place. Don't say something that can't be understood, hoping it'll be understood later. And don't say, when I have free time I'll study, because maybe you won't.
Look at the middle one. Makom in Hebrew: his place, his spot, where he's standing. Not until you've heard about it.

Now the line right before it: don't be sure of yourself until the day you die. The Talmud tells of a high priest who served faithfully for eighty years, and then, at the very end, left the path of the sages.
Nobody is beyond slipping. Put the two lines side by side: you can't be too sure about yourself, and you can't be too sure about the other person.
You don't know how you'd act in their place, because you've never stood there. Some teachers point out something quietly radical in the wording.
Can you ever really reach another person's place? Their childhood, their body, their worst morning?
Maybe never completely. Which would mean the judgment always waits. That doesn't mean anything goes; Jewish law has courts and judges.
But in everyday life, Hillel asks for a pause, and a little humility, before the verdict.

how: Hillel's warning is studied alongside the teaching to judge every person favorably, as a daily habit of thought.

o: place: where a person is standing
the community you must not leave
a court where judges hear a case

games.q: what's inside the saying — tap the pairs.
p: eighty years, then left the path

s: Hillel says to judge once you've heard their story
he says until you've reached his place, not heard about it.
the Talmud tells of a high priest who served eighty years, then strayed
a warning that nobody is beyond slipping.
Hillel says separate yourself from those who disappoint you
his first warning is don't separate yourself from the community.

games.q: a coworker has been late three times this month, and the whole office is talking. what does Hillel say?
o: hold the judgment. you haven't been in their place.
games.why: don't judge your fellow until you've reached his place, Hillel says, and don't be too sure of yourself either.

practice: Think of one person you've judged lately, and don't argue about whether you were right. Imagine waking up in their bed this morning: their worries, their body, their bank account, the conversation they're dreading.
Walk slowly through their morning until the moment you judged, and notice if anything shifts.

wordCard.voice: Makom. His place, where he stands: the word in Hillel's warning not to judge your fellow until you've reached it.

orig.note: Mishnaic Hebrew: until you reach his place.

carryVoice: Your line: nobody is beyond slipping. Not them, and not you either. That's day two hundred fifty-three.
